title: When a neighbor's cup breaks
hookLine: when someone else's cup breaks we say "these things happen," so say it of your own (Enchiridion 26)
tomorrow: A target isn't set up to be missed

cards: A friend texts: I dented my car backing out of the garage. Your reply takes four seconds. Oh no!
Happens to everyone. Is anyone hurt? That's what matters.
Wise, calm, kind. A week later you dent your own car backing out of your own garage, and for the next hour you're a different person. Idiot.
How could I. This always happens to me. Same kind of dent, same kind of morning.

teach.b: What nature intends, Epictetus says, we can learn from the cases where we all agree. Not from arguments, but from our own easy answers about other people's troubles.
When someone else's servant breaks a cup, people are quick to say: these things happen. So, he says, when your own cup breaks, be the same as you were when the other one broke. That's all.
Borrow your own good advice. Then he carries it further, gently but firmly. When someone else's child or spouse dies, everyone says: that's the human lot.
But when it's one's own, right away it's: oh, poor me, how wretched.
We ought to remember, he says, how we felt when we heard the same news about others. Here it's worth slowing down, because this is a hard line to hear.

Epictetus asks a great deal: the same steadiness for your own loss as for a stranger's. Not every reader will follow him that far, and nobody here is asked to. But the part anyone can use is narrower.
It's the doubled suffering, the sense that this, unlike everyone else's, shouldn't have happened, that the world has made an exception of you.
Often the wise, steady friend who knows exactly what to say about broken cups is already in the room. It's you, talking to someone else.
The trick is to turn around and say it to yourself, with the same warmth. It's strangely close to the old rule about loving your neighbor as yourself, only running backward.
Treat yourself, for a moment, as you'd treat your neighbor.
These things happen. To them. To you.

how: Some Stoic practitioners treat their own setbacks the way they would a friend's, using the same calm words they would readily offer someone else.

o: a drinking vessel shared at a Stoic banquet
a prized family heirloom that must never be broken
a broken thing we shrug off for others but not ourselves

games.q: when a neighbor's cup breaks — tap the pairs.

s: Epictetus says we can learn what nature intends from cases where we all agree
our easy answers about other people's troubles.
Epictetus asks for one calm for others' troubles and another for your own
he asks for the same: be as you were when the other cup broke.
the advice is to treat your own trouble as you would a neighbor's
the same words, the same calm.

games.q: you've just broken your favorite cup. last week your neighbor broke one, and you said: these things happen. what does Epictetus suggest now?
o: this time it's different; it was yours.
be the same as when the other cup broke.
games.why: when your own cup breaks, he says, be the same as when another's broke.

practice: Bring to mind one manageable trouble of your own, a mistake, a breakage, a bad week, and imagine a friend telling you that exact story as if it happened to them. Let your words for them come, kind and steady.
Then turn them around and say them to yourself, in the same tone: these things happen.

wordCard.voice: Cup. When a neighbor's breaks, Epictetus says, we're quick with calm and good advice; turn that same wisdom on your own. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: these things happen. The kind friend was in the room all along. Day three hundred fifty-eight, done.
